title: Quality Is a Plan of Checks Placed Before the Work Is Covered
summary: Quality is a planned system: a quality plan, inspection and test plans for each package, hold points that stop work until a written release, mock-ups of the hardest details, and nonconformance reports closed with evidence. Special inspection adds the code's own layer.
body:
Quality is not the absence of defects; it is a planned system of checks, placed before the work is covered, that proves each part meets the specification. The owner's job is to make sure the plan exists, that the checks that matter cannot be skipped, and that every failure is recorded and closed.

Recall

Q. Under an Incoterms rule, what does the purchase order still need to state separately?

A. When title passes, because Incoterms allocate cost, risk and customs duties but do not decide ownership.

Q. Why are connections the heart of a steel frame's safety?

A. Because the load path runs through them; force changes direction and concentrates at each connection, so a weak connection makes a weak structure.

Q. What does a design stage gate do?

A. It stops the design from advancing until defined deliverables are complete and approved, so later stages are not built on unresolved decisions.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, most defects that cost real money are not dramatic. They are a missing flashing, a weld nobody tested, a firestop never installed above a ceiling, concrete cover too thin by a few millimetres. Each is cheap to prevent before it is covered and expensive to find afterwards. As owner, you pay for the defect either way: in rework during construction, in warranty fights after, or in a lower price when a buyer's engineer finds it. Ingrid teaches the system that finds defects while they are still cheap.

The quality plan

In plain English: a written statement of how the contractor will make sure the work meets the specification, and how anyone can check that it did.

A project quality plan names the people responsible for quality, the procedures they follow, the inspections and tests for each type of work, how materials are approved and traced, how defects are recorded and closed, and how records are kept and handed over. It is usually written by the contractor and accepted by the owner. It sits beside the owner's own quality assurance, which checks that the contractor's quality control is actually happening. Quality control is checking the work; quality assurance is checking the checking. Those two words are often used loosely, and it pays to be precise.

Inspection and test plans, hold points and witness points

In plain English: a checklist for each type of work that says what will be checked, when, by whom, against what standard, and which checks must be passed before work continues.

The first new term: inspection and test plan (ITP), a table for one work package, for example cast-in-place concrete, listing each activity in sequence, the requirement it must meet, the inspection or test method, the frequency, the acceptance criteria, the responsible person, and the record produced. The second term: hold point, a step in the ITP at which work must stop until a named party has inspected and released it in writing. A witness point is lighter: the named party is notified and may attend, but work may continue if it does not. The difference is everything. A hold point is a gate; a witness point is an invitation.

A worked example, with a hypothetical concrete slab. The ITP lists: formwork line and level, a witness point for the contractor's engineer; reinforcement size, spacing and cover, a hold point for the engineer of record's representative and the special inspector; embedded conduits and sleeves, a witness point for the electrical and mechanical trades; pre-pour sign-off, a hold point for the contractor's superintendent; concrete delivery tickets and slump, tested on site; cylinders made for strength testing, at a frequency set by the specification; and curing, checked daily for seven days. If the reinforcement hold point is skipped and the cover is short, the defect is now under 200 millimetres of concrete. Before the pour, it was a ten-minute fix with a few bar chairs.

Say that out loud now.

Mock-ups: agreeing what good looks like

In plain English: build a small piece of the real thing first, test it and approve it, so everyone knows the standard before the whole building is built to it.

A mock-up is a full-size sample of a building element, such as a section of facade with a window, a corner, a roof edge, or a finished bathroom, built with the real materials, crews and methods. It may be tested, for example for water penetration under a standard field test, and once approved it becomes the reference for the rest of the work. A good mock-up deliberately includes the hardest details: the corner, the transition between two systems, the penetration. A mock-up of the easy middle of a wall teaches nothing.

A second worked example, hypothetical. A facade mock-up costs 60,000 dollars and takes 4 weeks. It fails a water test at the window-to-wall joint. The detail is changed and retested at a further 15,000 dollars. The building has 400 windows. Had the failure been found after installation, repairing each joint from a swing stage might cost 1,500 dollars, or 600,000 dollars in total, plus interior damage and tenant disruption. The mock-up and retest cost 75,000 dollars and found it on day one.

Nonconformance: recording failure honestly

The third new term: nonconformance report (NCR), a formal record that work, material or a document does not meet the requirement, with its cause, the proposed disposition, such as repair, replace, or accept as is with the designer's written approval, and the verification that the fix was done. An NCR is not an accusation. A project with no NCRs is not a perfect project; it is a project where nobody is writing them down. Owners should watch the NCR log for patterns, for how long NCRs stay open, and for any NCR closed as accept as is without a designer's signature.

Special inspections

The building code adds its own layer. For critical work, such as structural concrete, structural steel, high-strength bolting, welding, soils and certain fire-resistant materials, the code requires special inspection by a qualified inspector, engaged for the owner rather than the contractor, in addition to the building official's own inspections. Ivo covers the rules on Day 4. For now, know that special inspection is part of the quality system, not a replacement for it.

How the best do it

The strongest contractors treat quality as a production discipline. Before any work package starts, they hold a preparatory meeting with the foreman, the inspector and the designer, walk the ITP, agree the hardest details and build the first piece as a reviewed sample. They track NCRs by trade and cause, and they measure first-time pass rates at hold points. A small developer can copy that directly: require a pre-start meeting for every major package, a first-installation review, and a monthly NCR summary showing open items, age and repeat causes.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: rework costs may be treated differently from original construction costs for capitalisation; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: quality records are your evidence in any defect claim. Banking: lenders' monitors read NCR logs and special inspection reports before funding draws. Governance: accept-as-is decisions belong in the owner's decision log with the designer's signature. Estate: none directly. Exit: a buyer's due diligence will ask for the final special inspection report and the closed NCR log.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a hold point that can be passed by default when the inspector is late. The control is a written rule that work at a hold point stops until a written release, combined with a booking procedure and response time agreed with every inspector.

The beginner's mistake

Measuring quality by the number of NCRs and rewarding a project for having few. Few NCRs often means few inspections.

Callback

Last week, Quincy insisted on a witnessed factory acceptance test before equipment ships. That test is simply a hold point placed in a factory. The logic is identical: stop at the point after which a defect becomes expensive, and release only on evidence.

Recap

A quality plan sets the system. Inspection and test plans list every check, and hold points stop the work until a written release. Mock-ups agree the standard on the hardest details. NCRs record failures honestly and must be closed with evidence. Special inspection adds the code's own layer.

Next: Ford, with Cole, on Failure Forensics: Grenfell Tower and the difference between a certificate and evidence.
checklist: The contractor's quality plan is accepted before work starts.
Every major work package has an inspection and test plan.
Hold points are marked, named and require a written release.
Inspectors have an agreed booking procedure and response time.
Mock-ups include the hardest details, and the approved mock-up is kept as the reference.
I receive a monthly NCR summary with age, cause and repeat items.
No NCR is closed as accept as is without the designer's signature.
Special inspection is engaged for the owner, not the contractor.
head: Field checklist
speak: Quality is a plan of checks placed before work is covered. The contractor's quality plan names who is responsible, how materials are approved, how defects are recorded and how records are handed over. For each work package, an inspection and test plan lists every check, the standard, the frequency and the record. Some checks are witness points, where an inspector may attend. The important ones are hold points, where work stops until a named person releases it in writing. Reinforcement before a pour is the classic hold point: a ten-minute fix before the pour, a buried defect after. Mock-ups set the standard on the hardest details, like a window-to-wall joint, and in a hypothetical case a 75,000 dollar mock-up and retest avoided about 600,000 dollars of repairs. Nonconformance reports record every failure with its fix and its verification. And special inspection adds the building code's own layer, engaged for the owner.
terms: Inspection and test plan — a table for one work package listing each check, its standard, frequency, acceptance criteria, responsible person and record.
Hold point — a step at which work must stop until a named party inspects and releases it in writing.
Nonconformance report — a formal record that work or material fails a requirement, with its cause, disposition and verified fix.

hostile.q: Your hold points are costing the contractor waiting time. Why not make them witness points and let the inspector catch up?
hostile.a: Because a hold point exists exactly where a defect becomes buried and expensive, like reinforcement before a pour. Converting it to a witness point means accepting the risk of pouring over a defect. The fix for waiting time is a booking procedure with agreed response times, which we have, and I will review any hold point where the inspector has missed the agreed time.

title: Grenfell Tower: A Certificate Is a Claim, Not Evidence
summary: In June 2017 fire spread up the cladding of Grenfell Tower in London, killing 72 people. The 2024 inquiry report found a combustible cladding system accepted on misleading claims and weak testing and certification. The lesson for any owner is to accept products only on tests of the exact assembly being built.
body:
On 14 June 2017, fire spread up the outside of Grenfell Tower in London and 72 people died. The public inquiry's final report, published in September 2024, found that the cladding system installed in a refurbishment was combustible, and that misleading product claims, weak testing and certification, and failures across designers, contractors and regulators allowed it on the building.

Recall

Q. What is a hold point?

A. A step in an inspection and test plan at which work must stop until a named party has inspected and released it in writing.

Q. What is the root cause of most procurement failures?

A. Treating procurement as buying a price rather than delivering an accepted item to a need date, with no single owner for the whole chain.

Q. What is a nonconformance report?

A. A formal record that work or material fails a requirement, with its cause, disposition and the verification that the fix was made.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is a British case, and British regulations are not your design basis. Its lesson is universal. The products on that building arrived with certificates, test references and marketing claims, and many people accepted those papers as proof. Ford takes the case through seven steps, with Cole on the integrity of evidence, because quality systems fail most often not at the site but at the moment someone accepts a document instead of checking what it actually proves.

1. Timeline

Grenfell Tower was a residential tower block built in the 1970s. Between 2015 and 2016 it was refurbished, and the work added an external cladding system: aluminium composite material panels with a polyethylene core, fixed over combustible insulation, with a ventilated cavity behind. In the early hours of 14 June 2017, a fire started in a kitchen appliance in one flat. It spread into the cladding and travelled rapidly up and around the outside of the building. Residents had been told, under the building's fire strategy, to stay in their flats. Seventy-two people died. A public inquiry was established. Its first phase reported in 2019 on the night of the fire, and its second phase, on how the building came to be in that condition, reported on 4 September 2024.

2. Key decisions

The decisive decisions were the choice of cladding panel and insulation, and the acceptance of those choices by the design team, the contractor and building control. The inquiry found that a cheaper panel was chosen and that the decision was not tested against the fire performance the building needed. Each party accepted the products largely on the strength of certificates, test claims and the assurances of others.

3. Assumptions

The working assumption was that a product sold for use on tall buildings, with certificates and test references, was suitable for this building. The inquiry found that test results had been presented in misleading ways, that some products were marketed with claims that did not match how they had performed in testing, and that tests of one configuration were relied on for different configurations. A test proves the performance of the exact assembly that was tested, nothing more. That is the assumption that failed.

Say that out loud now.

4. Incentives

The inquiry described manufacturers with commercial incentives to present products favourably, certification and testing bodies that depended on fees from the firms whose products they assessed, consultants who assumed responsibility lay with others, and a regulatory regime that had not acted on earlier warnings. Cole's point: when the party paying for an assessment is the party being assessed, the owner must treat the result as a claim to be verified, not as independent evidence.

5. Warning signs ignored

The inquiry found that the dangers of combustible cladding on tall buildings had been known for years before 2017, including from earlier fires, and that warnings had not been acted on by government or industry. On the project itself, questions about the fire performance of the materials were raised and not resolved before installation. A question about fire performance that is answered with a certificate rather than a test of the actual assembly is a warning sign.

6. Point of no return

For the building, the point of no return was installation. Once the panels and insulation were on the facade, the hazard was permanent until removed, and the building's stay-put fire strategy assumed a facade that would not carry fire. For the residents, the night of the fire showed what happens when an assumption built into the whole life of a building is false.

7. Root cause

The inquiry's findings describe many contributing failures, so a single root cause is a simplification. For a developer, the operating lesson is this: product acceptance rested on documents whose meaning nobody verified. Nobody asked, clearly enough and early enough, whether the exact system to be installed had been tested in the configuration it would be built, and whether the tester was independent of the seller.

Cole's view: reading a certificate

Cole reads every product certificate with five questions. What exactly was tested, down to the components, thicknesses and fixings? Under which standard and which edition? By whom, and who paid? Does the tested configuration match what will be installed? Is the claimed use within the scope of the test? A certificate that cannot answer all five is marketing. A worked example, hypothetical: a cladding panel certificate references a fire test of the panel over a non-combustible backing. The project proposes the same panel over a combustible insulation with a cavity. The certificate says nothing about that assembly. Accepting it would be accepting a claim about a different product.

A second worked example: the cost of the check

Hypothetical figures. An independent fire engineer's review of a facade system's test evidence costs perhaps 20,000 dollars and two weeks. A full-scale facade fire test of a proposed assembly, where one is needed, costs far more and takes months. Against the cost of removing and replacing a facade, or worse, the review is trivial. The point is that the cheapest control, reading the evidence properly, comes first.

Substitution: where good evidence goes bad

Much of the danger in a case like this sits in substitution. A design is often specified with one product and built with another, chosen for price or availability. Every substitution is a new product approval, and the evidence that supported the original choice does not transfer. Owners can control this cheaply: the specification states that any substitution of a fire-rated, structural or envelope product needs a formal request, the same evidence package as the original, and the design professional's written acceptance. A substitution request that arrives with a brochure and a price saving, and nothing else, should be returned unread. Cole adds that the record of each substitution, who proposed it, what evidence was offered and who accepted it, is exactly what an investigator or a buyer's engineer will ask for years later. If that record does not exist, the owner cannot show that anyone checked.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is accepting a product on a certificate that does not test the assembly you are building. The control is a product approval procedure that requires the five answers above, reviewed by an independent qualified professional for any life-safety element. Professional sign-off required: a fire protection engineer for facade and fire-resistant assemblies.

The beginner's mistake

Believing that more paperwork means more safety. Many papers that each test something else prove nothing about your wall.

Callback

In Week 102, Magnus taught the fire strategy as a system: sprinklers, compartments, alarms and the assumption that fire is contained where it starts. Grenfell shows that the facade is part of that system. A strategy that assumes containment fails if the exterior can carry fire past every compartment.

Recap

Grenfell Tower burned in 2017 after a refurbishment installed a combustible cladding system, and 72 people died. The 2024 inquiry report found misleading product claims, weak testing and certification, and failures across the industry and regulators. Rule 116 makes the test of the exact assembly the only acceptable evidence.

Next: Roman on The Money: the cost of quality, and why prevention is the cheapest line in the budget.
checklist: Every life-safety product is approved against a test of the exact assembly being installed.
I ask what was tested, under which standard, by whom, and who paid.
The tested configuration is compared with the installed configuration in writing.
A fire protection engineer reviews facade and fire-resistant assembly evidence.
Product substitutions are re-approved against the same evidence test.
Unresolved fire-performance questions stop installation.
I treat certificates paid for by the seller as claims to verify.
head: Field checklist
speak: On 14 June 2017, fire spread up the outside of Grenfell Tower in London, and 72 people died. A refurbishment had added cladding panels with a polyethylene core over combustible insulation. The inquiry's final report, published in September 2024, found misleading product claims and test results, weak testing and certification, consultants and contractors who assumed others were responsible, and earlier warnings that were not acted on. It is a British case, not my design basis, but the lesson is universal: a test proves the performance only of the exact assembly that was tested. So before I accept any life-safety product, I ask five questions: what was tested, under which standard, by whom, who paid, and whether the tested configuration matches what we will build. A certificate that cannot answer them is marketing. A fire protection engineer reviews the evidence. My rule: accept a product only on a test of the assembly we are building.
terms: Aluminium composite material — panels of two thin aluminium sheets bonded to a core, which may be combustible depending on its composition.
Stay-put strategy — a fire strategy in which residents remain in their homes because fire is expected to be contained where it starts.
Tested configuration — the exact arrangement of components, thicknesses and fixings that a test actually assessed.

hostile.q: The facade supplier has a full set of certificates. Why are you paying an independent fire engineer to review them?
hostile.a: Because a certificate proves only what was tested. I need to know that the exact assembly we are building, with our insulation, cavity and fixings, has been tested for our use, and that the testing was independent. The review costs a fraction of a facade replacement, and on a life-safety element I will not accept a document whose meaning nobody has checked.

rule: Rule 116: Accept a life-safety product only on independent evidence that the exact assembly being built was tested for its use; a certificate or brochure is a claim, not evidence.

title: The Cost of Quality: Pay to Prevent, or Pay More to Fix
summary: Quality costs fall into prevention, appraisal, internal failure and external failure. Cutting prevention and inspection usually saves a little and costs a lot in rework, critical-path delay and a lower sale price. Price any proposed cut against the failure cost it creates.
body:
Quality has a price on both sides of the ledger. Money spent on prevention and checking is visible and easy to cut; money lost to rework, delay, warranty claims and a lower sale price is larger, later and hidden. The owner's job is to move money from the second column to the first.

Recall

Q. What five questions does Cole ask of a product certificate?

A. What exactly was tested, under which standard and edition, by whom and who paid, whether the tested configuration matches what will be installed, and whether the claimed use is within the test's scope.

Q. What is landed cost?

A. The full cost of an item delivered to site and cleared: price, packing, freight, insurance, duty, import tax, brokerage, port and inland charges, plus currency and early-payment costs.

Q. What does a mock-up do that a drawing cannot?

A. It shows, at full size with real materials and crews, what the agreed standard looks like on the hardest details, and it can be tested before the rest of the work is built.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, when a budget is tight, the inspection allowance and the mock-up are the first lines someone proposes to cut, because their benefit is invisible on the day you cut them. Roman's job is to make that benefit visible, in the same dollars as everything else, so the decision is made on numbers rather than optimism.

The cost of quality

In plain English: you can pay to prevent defects, pay to find them, or pay to fix them, and fixing them late is the most expensive of all.

The professional framing is the cost-of-quality model, long used in manufacturing and adapted to construction. It sorts quality costs into four groups. Prevention costs: the quality plan, design reviews, preparatory meetings, training and mock-ups. Appraisal costs: inspections, testing, special inspection and the lender's monitor. Internal failure costs: rework, scrap and delay found before handover. External failure costs: defects found after handover, such as warranty repairs, claims, legal costs, tenant losses and the discount a buyer demands. The insight practitioners take from the model is directional: a dollar moved into prevention usually saves several dollars of failure, and failure found after handover is the most expensive of all. The exact ratio varies by project, so treat any published multiplier with caution.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. A 30,000,000 dollar project budgets 450,000 dollars for prevention and appraisal: 1.5 percent. Someone proposes cutting it to 150,000 dollars. Roman models two outcomes. With the full allowance, he estimates internal failure at 300,000 dollars and external failure at 200,000 dollars, a total quality cost of 950,000 dollars. With the cut, he estimates internal failure at 700,000 dollars and external failure at 900,000 dollars, a total of 1,750,000 dollars. The cut saves 300,000 dollars and costs 1,100,000 dollars more in failure. These estimates are judgement, not data, and Roman says so; but even if he is wrong by half, the cut loses money.

Say that out loud now.

What rework does to the schedule and the loan

In plain English: rework costs twice, once for the repair and once for the time the repair takes.

Rework on the critical path adds cost of carry: construction interest, general conditions and forgone net operating income (NOI), which is income less operating expenses before debt service. A second worked example, hypothetical. Inspectors find that fire-stopping was omitted at service penetrations on three floors after ceilings were closed. Opening, fire-stopping, re-inspecting and closing the ceilings costs 90,000 dollars directly. Because the ceilings were on the critical path to the final fire inspection, the work adds 3 weeks. At a cost of carry of 100,000 dollars a week, that is 300,000 dollars. Total cost of the omission: 390,000 dollars. The fire-stopping itself, done before ceilings closed, would have cost perhaps 25,000 dollars, and a hold point before ceiling closure would have caught it.

Quality and value at exit

A buyer's due diligence team reads the special inspection reports, the NCR log and the warranty files. An incomplete record does not prove a defect, but it removes the buyer's confidence, and the buyer prices that loss of confidence. Suppose a stabilised building has NOI of 2,000,000 dollars and a buyer's cap rate of 6 percent, which gives a value of about 33,300,000 dollars. A buyer who finds open NCRs on the facade and no final special inspection report might hold back a hypothetical 1,000,000 dollars for investigation and repair, or raise its required return. Either way, missing paper becomes a lower price. Good records are an asset at sale.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

Latent defects follow ownership. On your personal balance sheet, a building you sold can still carry contingent liability through warranties, indemnities or claims, depending on the contract and the law; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. The cheapest way to shrink that contingent liability is a quality record that shows the work was inspected and closed. A licensed adviser is required before you act on any related insurance or structure.

Where the quality money should go

Not every package deserves the same spending. Roman ranks packages by two questions: how much does a defect here cost if it is found late, and how likely is a defect given the trade, the complexity and the contractor's history? Envelope transitions, fire-stopping, structural connections, waterproofing below grade and building services above closed ceilings usually rank high on both. Painting and finishes rank lower, because their defects are visible and cheap to fix. Spending is then weighted toward the high-ranked packages: more hold points, earlier mock-ups, continuous rather than periodic inspection where the code allows the choice. A worked example, hypothetical. A 450,000 dollar quality budget is split evenly across 15 packages, 30,000 dollars each. Roman reallocates it so the five high-risk packages receive 60,000 dollars each, 300,000 dollars in total, and the other ten share 150,000 dollars, 15,000 dollars each. The total does not change; the protection does, because the money now sits where a late-found defect would cost the most.

What the lender's monitor reads

Lenders care about quality for a simple reason: a defect that delays completion or reduces value threatens repayment. A lender's monitor will typically read the special inspection reports, the NCR log and its ageing, and the status of any accept-as-is decisions before supporting a draw. A clean, current quality record makes draws routine. A record with old open NCRs on structural or envelope work invites questions, deferred amounts and sometimes a retention against the cost of the fix. Quality evidence is therefore also cash-flow evidence, and treating it that way is the simplest argument for funding it properly.

Monthly thread: decision journals

Quality spending is a decision made under uncertainty, with the result arriving years later, which makes it ideal for a decision journal. When you set or cut a quality budget, write down the date, what you decided, the failure cost you expected, and why. At close-out, compare the entry with the defect log.

Ask yourself: on your last major decision about spending to prevent a problem, what did you expect, and would you be willing to have that expectation checked against what actually happened?

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is cutting prevention and appraisal to protect a budget line, then paying for failure from contingency and sale price. The control is to require any proposed cut to quality spending to come with a cost-of-quality estimate showing the expected failure cost it creates.

The beginner's mistake

Counting only the direct cost of rework and forgetting the schedule time it consumes on the critical path.

Callback

In Week 107, Zara and Quincy taught life-cycle cost: the cheapest first cost can be the most expensive building to own. The cost-of-quality model is the same idea over the construction period. Prevention is a higher first cost that buys a lower total cost.

Recap

Quality costs fall into prevention, appraisal, internal failure and external failure. Prevention is cheapest, and failure after handover is most expensive. Rework costs both repair and critical-path time. Good records protect value at sale and reduce contingent liability after it.

Next: Ivo on The Rules: special inspections under the building code, and the owner's right to reject and uncover work.
checklist: I know the project's budget for prevention and appraisal as a percentage of cost.
Any proposed cut to quality spending comes with a cost-of-quality estimate.
Rework is priced with its critical-path delay, not just the repair.
A hold point sits before every covering operation, such as closing ceilings.
Quality records are organised as an asset for sale.
I know which warranties and indemnities follow me after sale.
Estimates of failure cost are labelled as judgement, not data.
head: Field checklist
speak: Quality costs money on both sides. Prevention, like the quality plan, preparatory meetings and mock-ups, and appraisal, like inspection and testing, are visible and easy to cut. Internal failure, meaning rework before handover, and external failure, meaning defects after handover, are larger and later. In a hypothetical project, cutting a 450,000 dollar quality budget to 150,000 saved 300,000 dollars and was estimated to add 1,100,000 dollars of failure. Rework also costs time: fire-stopping missed above closed ceilings cost 90,000 dollars to fix plus three critical-path weeks, 390,000 dollars in total, for work that would have cost 25,000 dollars if a hold point had caught it. And at sale, missing inspection reports and open defect records become a lower price. So I require any cut to quality spending to come with an estimate of the failure it creates, and I keep the quality record as an asset.
terms: Cost of quality — the total of prevention, appraisal, internal failure and external failure costs.
Internal failure cost — the cost of defects found and fixed before handover, including rework and delay.
External failure cost — the cost of defects found after handover, such as warranty repairs, claims and lost value.

hostile.q: You are spending 1.5 percent of the budget on inspection and mock-ups. Why should I not cut that to fund the overrun?
hostile.a: Because it would move cost, not remove it. Our estimate is that cutting it to 0.5 percent saves 300,000 dollars and adds more than 1,000,000 dollars in rework, delay and post-handover defects, and those estimates are judgement, so I have shown them as a range. Even at the low end the cut loses money. I would rather fund the overrun from the contingency line it belongs to.

title: Special Inspections and the Right to Reject
summary: The building code requires special inspection of critical work under a statement prepared by the design professional, by inspectors engaged for the owner. The contract lets the owner reject defective work and require uncovering, with cost following what is found. Accepting nonconforming work needs the designer's written approval.
body:
The building code requires special inspection of critical work by a qualified inspector working for the owner, under a written statement prepared by the design professional, and the contract gives the owner the right to reject defective work and to require covered work to be uncovered. Knowing both lets you act on a defect without starting a fight you will lose.

Recall

Q. What are the four groups in the cost-of-quality model?

A. Prevention, appraisal, internal failure and external failure.

Q. What is a vesting clause?

A. A contract term stating when title to goods or work passes to the owner, for example on payment or on marking and segregation.

Q. What is the difference between quality control and quality assurance?

A. Quality control checks the work; quality assurance checks that the quality control is actually happening.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, when a defect is found, two questions decide what happens next: what does the law require, and what does the contract allow you to demand? A developer who knows the answers can stop the work, require a fix and keep the cost where it belongs. One who does not can find that he has ordered work he must pay for, or accepted work he cannot later reject.

Special inspection under the building code

In plain English: for certain critical work, the code demands an extra, independent inspector, paid for by the owner, on top of the building official's inspections.

The professional framing is the special inspection chapter of the International Building Code (IBC), Chapter 17 in recent editions, as adopted in your jurisdiction. Verify against the current adopted edition. Its main features, as generally understood, are these. The registered design professional in responsible charge prepares a statement of special inspections listing the work that needs special inspection or testing, the frequency, and who will perform it, and it is submitted as part of the permit process [unverified — confirm independently]. The owner, or the owner's agent, engages the special inspectors, not the contractor, so that the inspector is independent of the party being inspected [unverified — confirm independently]. Inspection is either continuous, with the inspector present throughout the work, or periodic, at stated intervals. Inspectors keep records, report discrepancies to the contractor for correction, and, if uncorrected, to the design professional and the building official. A final report documents the inspections and the correction of any discrepancies, and the building official generally relies on it before issuing a certificate of occupancy.

A new term: statement of special inspections, the design professional's written list of what must be specially inspected or tested, how often, and by whom.

A worked example. The statement lists continuous special inspection for complete-penetration welds on a moment frame and periodic inspection for high-strength bolting. The contractor schedules welding on a weekend without booking the inspector. On Monday the inspector finds the welds were made without continuous inspection. The welds are not automatically defective, but they were not inspected as required. The likely path is non-destructive testing of the completed welds, at a hypothetical 8,000 dollars, paid by the contractor if the contract makes it responsible for scheduling, and a written report to the design professional. The owner's role is to make sure the discrepancy is recorded and closed, not quietly forgotten.

Say that out loud now.

Testing standards the inspector applies

Special inspectors work to referenced standards. For concrete, ASTM C31 governs how test cylinders are made and cured in the field and ASTM C39 governs how they are tested for compressive strength, and acceptance of strength is set by ACI 318 and the project specification. For welding, AWS D1.1 sets inspection requirements, and inspectors are commonly qualified as certified welding inspectors. Soils work references compaction test standards from ASTM. Verify each edition against the current adopted edition. The owner does not need to know the contents; he needs to see that the specification names them and that the testing agency is accredited for them.

The contract: rejecting and uncovering work

In plain English: the owner can refuse defective work, and can make the contractor open up finished work to check it, but who pays depends on what is found.

Standard American contract forms, such as the AIA general conditions, typically give the owner, through the architect, the right to reject work that does not conform to the contract, and require the contractor to correct rejected work at its own cost. They also typically deal with uncovering: if work was covered contrary to a request to inspect it first, the contractor uncovers it at its own cost; if it was covered without such a request and is then found to conform, the owner usually pays for uncovering and replacing it; if it is found defective, the contractor pays. Verify the exact wording in your form and edition. ConsensusDocs and FIDIC contain comparable mechanisms with their own procedures.

A second worked example, hypothetical. The owner's representative suspects that the waterproofing membrane under a podium slab was not lapped correctly. The slab is poured. Opening a test area costs 20,000 dollars. If the membrane is found defective, the contractor pays the 20,000 dollars and the repair. If it conforms and the membrane was not a hold point the contractor ignored, the owner pays the 20,000 dollars. That is why the right answer is to make the membrane a hold point before the pour: it converts an expensive argument after the fact into a cheap inspection before it.

Accept as is: a decision with a signature

Sometimes the best answer to nonconforming work is to keep it, perhaps with a credit. That is a change to the contract and to the design, and it needs the design professional's written acceptance and, where the work is under special inspection or affects code compliance, the building official's agreement. Professional sign-off required: the engineer or architect of record for any accept-as-is decision on structural, fire or life-safety work.

Structural observation and the official's own inspections

Two other layers sit beside special inspection and are easy to confuse with it. The building official carries out its own required inspections at stages set by the code and the permit, such as foundations before placement and framing before cover. Separately, for some structures the code requires structural observation, a visual review by the registered design professional, or someone it designates, of general conformance of the structural system at significant stages [unverified — confirm independently]. Structural observation is not special inspection and does not replace it. Each layer has its own trigger, its own record and its own sign-off, and a project file should show all three. Verify against the current adopted edition which apply to your building.

The accredited testing agency

The laboratory that tests cylinders, soils or welds should be accredited for the specific tests it performs, often under a recognised accreditation scheme for testing laboratories. Ask for its scope of accreditation, not just its name. A laboratory accredited for soils but not concrete compression testing is the wrong laboratory for your slab, however good its brochure.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is letting the contractor engage and pay the special inspector. The control is an owner-held contract with an accredited inspection agency, with the statement of special inspections as its scope and reports going directly to the owner and the design professional.

The beginner's mistake

Ordering work to be uncovered without first checking the contract, then paying for the uncovering when the work turns out to be fine.

Callback

In Week 77, LEX and Marco taught notices and conditions precedent: a right not exercised in the stated way can be lost. Rejection and uncovering are rights of exactly that kind; exercise them in writing, through the stated channel, at the stated time.

Recap

The code requires special inspection of critical work under a statement of special inspections, by inspectors the owner engages. Inspectors apply named ASTM, ACI and AWS standards. The contract lets the owner reject defective work and require uncovering, with cost following the result. Accept-as-is needs the designer's signature.

Next: Ingrid on The Numbers: reverse engineering a defect log and a low strength result back to their causes.
checklist: A statement of special inspections exists and is part of the permit file.
The owner, not the contractor, engages the special inspection agency.
The testing agency is accredited for the standards it applies.
The specification names each referenced standard and its edition.
Inspection discrepancies are recorded and tracked to closure.
I check the contract before ordering covered work to be uncovered.
Accept-as-is decisions carry the design professional's signature.
The final report of special inspections is filed before occupancy.
head: Field checklist
speak: For critical work like structural concrete, steel, welding, bolting and soils, the building code requires special inspection on top of the official's own inspections. The design professional prepares a statement of special inspections listing what is inspected, how often and by whom, and the owner engages the inspectors, so they are independent of the contractor. Inspection is continuous or periodic, discrepancies go to the contractor and, if uncorrected, to the designer and the official, and a final report supports occupancy. Inspectors apply named standards, such as ASTM C31 and C39 for concrete cylinders, ACI 318 for acceptance, and AWS D1.1 for welds. Under the contract, the owner can reject defective work at the contractor's cost and can require covered work to be uncovered; if it conforms, the owner usually pays to uncover it. So I make critical items hold points before they are covered, and any accept-as-is needs the designer's signature.
terms: Statement of special inspections — the design professional's written list of work requiring special inspection or testing, its frequency and who performs it.
Continuous special inspection — inspection with the inspector present for the whole time the work is performed.
Accept as is — a decision to keep nonconforming work unchanged, usually with the designer's approval and often a credit.

hostile.q: You ordered us to open the podium slab and the membrane was fine. Why should the contractor pay for that?
hostile.a: It should not, and we will pay for the opening and reinstatement, because the work conformed and it was not a hold point you bypassed. That is exactly why we have now added a hold point before every membrane is covered: a cheap inspection beforehand instead of an argument afterwards. Please send the cost with the daily records and we will process it.

title: Reverse Engineering a Defect Log and a Low Break
summary: Start from the total rework cost and split it by where each defect was found; late-found defects reveal the missing hold points, and the extra inspections usually cost a fraction of the failure. For a low concrete strength result, the acceptance criterion that failed points to the cause.
body:
A finished defect log tells you where the quality system failed, if you read it backward. Start from the total cost of rework, split it by where each defect was found, and the pattern shows which hold points were missing; start from a low strength result, and the acceptance rules show which test failed and what to do next.

Recall

Q. Who engages the special inspector, and why?

A. The owner or the owner's agent, so that the inspector is independent of the contractor whose work is being inspected. Verify against the current adopted edition.

Q. What does a factory acceptance test protect against?

A. Shipping equipment that does not meet its specification or certification; a fault fixed at the works costs days, the same fault found on site can cost months.

Q. How do you reverse engineer picks per day for a steel frame?

A. Divide the number of pieces by the working days available, then by crane hours, and check whether the resulting time per pick is realistic with a weather allowance.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, at the end of every project you will receive a defect log and a pile of test reports. Most owners file them. Ingrid uses them to find the two or three changes that would have saved the most money, and carries those changes to the next project. This is an even week, so she starts from the finished outcome and works backward, with hypothetical round numbers.

The finished outcome

A hypothetical project has closed. The nonconformance log holds 120 closed NCRs. The total cost of rework, including direct repair and the cost of critical-path delay, was 1,800,000 dollars. The question is where it came from.

Step 1: split the cost by where each defect was found

Ingrid sorts each NCR by the stage at which the defect was found. Found at a hold point before covering: 70 NCRs, average cost 2,000 dollars, total 140,000 dollars. Found after covering but before handover: 35 NCRs, average cost 20,000 dollars, total 700,000 dollars. Found after handover, under warranty: 15 NCRs, average cost 64,000 dollars, total 960,000 dollars. Add them: 140,000 plus 700,000 plus 960,000 is 1,800,000 dollars. The 15 defects found after handover were 12.5 percent of the count and over half the cost.

Step 2: back out the cost multiplier by stage

The average defect found at a hold point cost 2,000 dollars. Found after covering, 10 times that. Found after handover, 32 times. These multipliers are from this hypothetical log, not a published rule, but the shape is what practitioners see: the later a defect is found, the more it costs, because more work sits on top of it and more people are affected by fixing it.

Say that out loud now.

Step 3: back out which hold points were missing

Ingrid now reads the 50 defects found after covering or after handover by work package. Suppose 22 were in fire-stopping and penetrations, 14 in envelope waterproofing at transitions, 8 in mechanical and electrical rough-in above ceilings, and 6 elsewhere. That points straight at the inspection and test plans: none of those packages had a hold point before the covering operation, closing ceilings or cladding over the membrane. Working backward, she estimates that hold points at those three moments would have caught perhaps two-thirds of those 50 defects at the hold-point stage. Two-thirds of 50 is about 33 defects. Their actual cost, using an average across the two late stages of about 33,000 dollars, was roughly 1,100,000 dollars. Caught at a hold point, they would have cost about 33 times 2,000 dollars, or 66,000 dollars. The saving would have been about 1,000,000 dollars.

Step 4: back out what the extra inspection would have cost

Three extra hold points in each of 10 work areas is 30 inspections, plus perhaps 30 more for re-inspections and other areas. At a hypothetical 800 dollars per inspection visit, 60 visits cost 48,000 dollars, plus a little waiting time for the trades. Against a saving of about 1,000,000 dollars, the return is roughly twenty to one. That is the number Ingrid carries to the next project's budget meeting.

A second worked example: a low strength result

Now reverse a single test. The specified compressive strength for a slab is 4,000 pounds per square inch. Under ACI 318, as commonly applied for that strength range, the concrete is accepted if every average of three consecutive strength tests equals or exceeds the specified strength, and no single test falls below it by more than 500 pounds per square inch [unverified — confirm independently]. A strength test is the average of the cylinders tested at the same age, usually 28 days. Verify the criteria and their exceptions against the current adopted edition.

The results for one placement sequence: 4,300, 3,900 and 3,700. The average of those three is 11,900 divided by 3, about 3,967, which is below 4,000, so the three-test criterion fails. The lowest single test, 3,700, is 300 below the specified strength, within the 500 allowance, so the single-test criterion passes. Working backward, the failure is a modest, consistent shortfall, not one bad batch. That points at the mix, the water added on site or the curing, rather than one truck. The next steps are usually an investigation, cores from the affected placement for testing, and the engineer of record's assessment of whether the in-place strength is adequate for the design. A low break is a question, not a verdict.

A second reading of the same data: if the results had been 4,400, 4,300 and 3,400, the average would be 4,033, passing the average criterion, but 3,400 is 600 below the specified strength, failing the single-test criterion. That pattern points at one batch or one set of cylinders, and possibly at how those cylinders were made, stored or handled under ASTM C31. Different failure pattern, different investigation.

Step 5: write the lesson into the next project

Ingrid turns the review into three concrete changes. First, the standard inspection and test plans for fire-stopping, envelope transitions and above-ceiling services each gain a hold point before covering, with the inspector named. Second, the contractor's monthly quality report must show NCRs by the stage at which they were found, so the shape of the log is visible during the project, not only at the end. Third, the budget for inspection is set from this project's measured multipliers, not from a rule of thumb. A finished log that changes nothing on the next job was a cost with no return.

A caution about the numbers

Every multiplier and saving here is hypothetical, and even a real log from one project is a small sample. Defects found after handover are also undercounted, because some are never reported and others are absorbed by tenants. So treat the reverse-engineered saving as a floor, not a forecast. The decision it supports does not need precision; it needs the direction, and the direction is consistent.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is filing the defect log without reading it backward, and repeating the same missing hold points on the next project. The control is a close-out review in which every late-found defect is assigned to the hold point that should have caught it, and the next project's inspection and test plans are amended.

The beginner's mistake

Judging quality by the number of defects instead of the stage at which they were found. Seventy defects caught at hold points is a system working; fifteen found under warranty is a system failing.

Callback

In Week 2, Kema taught after-action reviews: what was supposed to happen, what did happen, why, and what we will do differently. Reading the defect log backward is an after-action review with a cost attached to every lesson.

Recap

Split rework cost by the stage each defect was found. The later the stage, the higher the cost. Assign late defects to the missing hold points, price the extra inspections, and compare. For a low strength result, check which acceptance criterion failed and let the pattern direct the investigation.

Next: Ingrid on The Room: the morning the inspector is late and the contractor wants to pour past the hold point.
checklist: Every NCR records the stage at which the defect was found.
I split rework cost by stage at close-out.
Late-found defects are assigned to the hold point that should have caught them.
The next project's inspection and test plans are amended from the review.
The cost of extra inspections is compared with the failure cost they would avoid.
For a low break, I check which acceptance criterion failed before deciding the investigation.
Cores and the engineer of record's assessment come before any removal decision.
head: Field checklist
speak: A finished defect log tells me where the quality system failed if I read it backward. In a hypothetical project, 120 defects cost 1,800,000 dollars. Seventy found at hold points cost 2,000 dollars each. Thirty-five found after covering cost ten times that. Fifteen found after handover cost thirty-two times that, and those fifteen were over half the total. Reading the late ones by package, most were fire-stopping, envelope transitions and work above ceilings, none of which had a hold point before being covered. Adding about sixty inspections would have cost around 48,000 dollars and saved about a million. For a concrete low break, I check which acceptance criterion failed: a low average of three tests points to a consistent cause like the mix or curing, while one very low test points to one batch or the cylinders. Either way, a low break is a question for cores and the engineer, not a verdict.
terms: Strength test — the average strength of the cylinders made from one sample and tested at the same age, usually 28 days.
Close-out review — a structured review at project end that assigns each late-found defect to the control that should have caught it.
Cost multiplier by stage — the ratio of a defect's cost when found late to its cost when found at a hold point.

hostile.q: Three cylinder results average below the specified strength. Are you going to demolish the slab?
hostile.a: No. The average criterion failed by a small margin and no single test is far below, which points to a consistent cause such as the mix or curing rather than one bad batch. The next step is cores from that placement and the engineer of record's assessment of in-place strength against the design. We will decide on any remedy after that, and I will send you the coring plan this week.

title: The Inspector Is Late and the Trucks Are Batched
summary: The special inspector is an hour late and the superintendent wants to pour over reinforcement nobody has released. Hold the hold point, ask whether the inspector can release in stages, compare the bounded cost of waiting with the cost of a buried defect, and settle the standby cost by the booking record.
body:
The test of a quality system is the morning it is inconvenient. The pump truck is idling, the concrete is batched, the special inspector is an hour late, and the superintendent wants to start pouring over reinforcement nobody has released. The owner's answer has to be ready before that morning arrives.

Recall

Q. What does a defect log read backward tell you?

A. Which stage each defect was found at, what that cost, and which hold points were missing, so the next project's inspection plans can be amended.

Q. What is continuous special inspection?

A. Inspection with the inspector present for the whole time the work is performed, as required for certain critical work such as some welding.

Q. What does Rule 115 define as delivered?

A. An item that is on site, cleared, certified and accepted by the authority, not merely shipped.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a hold point that can be bypassed under pressure is a witness point with a grander name. Your contractor will rarely ask you to abolish a hold point. It will ask for one exception, on one morning, for a good reason. Ingrid shows you how to hold the line and keep the job moving.

The scene

Six in the morning on a hypothetical job. A slab pour is scheduled for seven. The reinforcement hold point requires written release by the special inspector. The inspector's office says she is stuck in traffic and will arrive about eight. Concrete trucks are already batched. The superintendent calls your owner's representative: the steel was checked yesterday by his own foreman, the mix will be wasted if it sits, and he wants permission to start pouring at the far end and have the inspector catch up. Your representative rings you.

The question behind the question

The superintendent's real question is whether the hold point is real. If you agree once, every hold point on the job becomes negotiable, and the next exception will come with less reason. His second, unspoken question is who carries the cost of the wasted concrete. That is a fair question, and it has a contractual answer you should know before you speak.

The lines to say

"I understand the pressure, and I want this pour today. The hold point stands: we do not place concrete over reinforcement that has not been released."

"Can the inspector release the first bay remotely from photos and the foreman's checklist, and then confirm on arrival before we pour past it? Ask her now; that is her call, not mine."

"Hold the trucks that are not yet loaded. Let us look at the booking record together afterwards and see why the inspector was late and who carries the cost under the contract."

Say that out loud now.

The lines never to say

"Go ahead, just this once." There is no just this once; the next request will cite it.

"Your foreman's check is good enough." It converts quality assurance into self-certification, which is what special inspection exists to prevent.

"We will deal with it if the inspector finds a problem." Once concrete is placed, the only way to find the problem is to break out the slab.

When to stay silent

After you say the hold point stands, stop. The superintendent will test the silence with his strongest argument. Let him make it, acknowledge it, and repeat the position once. Repeating calmly is more persuasive than explaining at length, which sounds like you are looking for a way out.

Holding your state

Your pulse will rise because money is visibly burning. Slow your breathing and your speech. The wasted cost of a delayed pour is bounded and known; the cost of a slab poured over defective reinforcement is neither. Say that sentence to yourself before you pick up the phone.

A worked example of the cost

Hypothetical figures. The pour is 150 cubic metres. Two trucks, 16 cubic metres, are already loaded and may exceed their allowed time before placement if held two hours; that concrete, at 200 dollars a cubic metre, is 3,200 dollars, plus a pump standby charge of 1,500 dollars and crew standby of 3,000 dollars. Worst case: 7,700 dollars. Now the other side. If the reinforcement cover is short over a 200 square metre bay, breaking out and replacing that bay could cost 60,000 dollars and two weeks. At a hypothetical cost of carry of 100,000 dollars a critical-path week, the downside is about 260,000 dollars. You are paying at most 7,700 dollars to avoid a risk of 260,000. Even a small chance of a defect makes the wait worth it.

A second check: who pays the 7,700 dollars? If the inspection booking was made on time and the inspector, engaged by the owner, was late, the owner may carry the standby cost. If the contractor booked late or failed to give the notice the procedure requires, it carries the cost. The booking record decides, which is why the procedure must require written booking with a stated notice period.

What happened next

The inspector reviewed photos of the first bay, released it remotely as a provisional release, and confirmed on site at 07:50 before the pour reached the second bay. She found two bundles of bar missing chairs, short on cover, in bay three. They were fixed in fifteen minutes. The pour finished by early afternoon. Ingrid's note for the file: the hold point worked, the booking procedure needs a backup inspector, and remote provisional release should be written into the inspection procedure rather than improvised, with the inspector's agreement.

Writing the rule before the morning

The morning went well because the rule was clear. Ingrid's inspection procedure for any critical pour now carries five lines. Inspection must be booked in writing at least the agreed notice before the pour. The inspector's office confirms the booking in writing. A named backup inspector is available on pour days. Where the inspector agrees, a provisional release of the first bay may be given from photographs and the foreman's checklist, confirmed in person before concrete passes that bay. No concrete is placed over reinforcement that has not been released, by any route. Those five lines are agreed with the contractor at the pre-start meeting for the concrete package, so on the morning itself nobody is negotiating. The superintendent is not your opponent; he is a professional under pressure who needs a rule he can point to when his own crew asks why they are waiting.

How to tell your owner's representative

Your representative rang you because he was not sure he had the authority. Give it to him in advance, in writing: he may hold any hold point without calling you, and he must call you before agreeing to any exception. That inverts the pressure. Holding becomes the easy default and an exception becomes the unusual act that needs a second person.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is an owner who has never decided in advance what happens when an inspector is late, and so decides under pressure. The control is a written inspection procedure covering booking notice, backup inspectors, remote provisional release where the inspector permits it, and who carries standby cost.

The beginner's mistake

Making the hold-point decision yourself. The release belongs to the named inspector; the owner's job is to protect the rule and fix the booking system.

Callback

Last week, Quincy kept payment tied to a passed factory test when a supplier wanted to ship. This is the same posture on site: the bounded cost of waiting is compared with the unbounded cost of a buried defect, and the gate holds until the evidence arrives.

Recap

Hold the hold point. Ask whether the inspector can release in stages. Hold unloaded trucks. Settle cost by the booking record afterwards. Compare the bounded cost of waiting with the cost of a buried defect, and fix the booking procedure so the morning does not repeat.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap: the week's six questions on quality, Cole's Auditor's Chair and the boardroom drill.
checklist: I decided in advance what happens when an inspector is late.
The inspection procedure requires written booking with a stated notice period.
A backup inspector is named for critical pours.
Remote provisional release is in the procedure only where the inspector agrees to it.
Loaded and unloaded trucks are managed separately during a delay.
Standby cost is settled from the booking record, not argued on the morning.
The release decision belongs to the named inspector, never to me.
head: Field checklist
speak: It is six in the morning, the trucks are batched, the special inspector is an hour late, and the superintendent wants to start pouring over reinforcement nobody has released. My answer is ready before that morning: the hold point stands. I ask whether the inspector can release the first bay from photos and the foreman's checklist and confirm on arrival, and I make clear that is her call, not mine. We hold the trucks not yet loaded. Then I stop talking and let the superintendent make his best argument, and I repeat the position once. The numbers make it easy: waiting costs at most a few thousand dollars in concrete and standby, while a buried defect could cost a bay replacement and two critical-path weeks. Afterwards, the booking record decides who pays the standby. And the procedure gets fixed: written booking, a backup inspector and agreed staged release.
terms: Provisional release — a staged or conditional release of a hold point by the inspector, confirmed by a later inspection before the work proceeds further.
Standby cost — the cost of crews, plant and materials kept waiting during a delay.
Booking procedure — the written process for requesting inspections, with notice periods and response times.

hostile.q: Your inspector was late, the concrete was wasted, and you held up my crew for two hours. Why should we not bill you for all of it?
hostile.a: If our inspector was late on a booking you made on time, the standby cost is ours, and we will pay it on the booking record. If the booking was late, it is yours. Either way the hold point was right: the inspector found short cover in bay three, which was fixed in fifteen minutes instead of a slab replacement. Send the standby cost with the booking record and we will settle it this week.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 116 Review: Hold Points, Evidence and Independence
summary: Six questions test the week: hold and witness points, inspection and test plans, the Grenfell lesson, the cost of quality, special inspection and reading a low break. Cole's Auditor's Chair finds eight defects in a hypothetical quality report, and the boardroom drill explains quality in two minutes.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: quality is proved by evidence gathered before the work is covered, so hold points must stop the work, products must be accepted on tests of the exact assembly, and every failure must be recorded, read and closed.

Recall

Q. What is the question behind a request to pour past a hold point?

A. Whether the hold point is real. Agreeing once makes every hold point negotiable; the honest secondary question is who carries the standby cost, which the booking record answers.

Q. What does Rule 115 say?

A. An item is not delivered until it is on site, cleared, certified and accepted by the authority.

Q. What are the three steps of the in-balance test logic in a construction loan?

A. Forecast the cost to complete, compare it with undisbursed loan plus undisbursed equity, and deposit any shortfall before the next draw.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, if you can answer these six questions without notes, you can read a contractor's quality plan, an inspection log and a product submittal and see where the risk is hiding. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. What is the difference between a hold point and a witness point?

Answer: At a hold point work must stop until a named party inspects and releases it in writing. At a witness point the party is notified and may attend, but work can continue if it does not.

Question 2. What does an inspection and test plan contain?

Answer: For one work package, each activity in sequence, the requirement, the inspection or test method, the frequency, the acceptance criteria, the responsible person and the record produced.

Question 3. What is the operating lesson of Grenfell Tower for a developer?

Answer: A certificate is a claim. Accept a life-safety product only on independent evidence that the exact assembly you are building was tested for its use. That is Rule 116.

Question 4. Name the four groups in the cost-of-quality model.

Answer: Prevention, appraisal, internal failure and external failure. Prevention is cheapest; failure found after handover is most expensive.

Question 5. Who prepares the statement of special inspections, and who engages the inspectors?

Answer: The registered design professional prepares it, and the owner or the owner's agent engages the inspectors so they are independent of the contractor. Verify against the current adopted edition.

Question 6. Three cylinder tests average below the specified strength but none is far below. What does that suggest, and what happens next?

Answer: A consistent shortfall, pointing to the mix, site water or curing rather than one batch. Next come an investigation, cores and the engineer of record's assessment of in-place strength.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Ingrid framed quality as a plan of checks before the work is covered: quality plans, inspection and test plans, hold points, mock-ups and NCRs. Ford and Cole took Grenfell Tower through seven steps, giving Rule 116. Roman priced the cost of quality and showed rework costing both repair and critical-path time. Ivo taught special inspection and the owner's rights to reject and uncover work. Ingrid reverse engineered a defect log and a low break. Ingrid ran the morning the inspector was late.

Cole's Auditor's Chair

Week 116 is a fourth week, so the Red Pen becomes Cole's Auditor's Chair: read this hypothetical monthly quality report as a hostile auditor would. Find the defects before reading on.

Monthly Quality Report, Month 9. Inspections completed: 140, all passed. NCRs raised this month: 0. Open NCRs: 6, all minor, oldest 11 weeks. NCR 41, waterproofing lap at podium: closed, accepted as is by site team. Level 6 slab: reinforcement inspected by contractor's foreman due to inspector unavailability; pour proceeded. Special inspection: contractor has engaged inspection agency to reduce cost. Facade: substitute insulation approved on supplier's certificate. Concrete: one set of cylinders not tested, cylinders damaged in storage. Prepared and approved by: Contractor's Quality Manager.

The auditor's findings. First, 140 inspections all passed with zero new NCRs is not reassurance; it suggests inspections are not finding things, or failures are not being written down. Second, six open NCRs with the oldest at 11 weeks shows no closure discipline, and minor is undefined. Third, NCR 41 was accepted as is by the site team, with no designer's signature, on a waterproofing item that is now buried. Fourth, the Level 6 pour bypassed a hold point on the foreman's say-so, which is self-certification; that slab's reinforcement now has no independent record. Fifth, the contractor engaging the inspection agency removes the independence special inspection is meant to provide. Sixth, a substitute insulation approved on a supplier's certificate is the Grenfell failure mode exactly; it needs a test of the installed assembly and a fire engineer's review. Seventh, damaged cylinders leave a placement with no strength record, which needs cores or other evidence. Eighth, the report is prepared and approved by the same person from the party being checked; it needs owner-side review.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week to a board in two minutes, then compare with the model answer.

Model answer: "Quality on our project is proved by evidence collected before work is covered. The contractor runs a quality plan with an inspection and test plan for each package, and the critical steps, like reinforcement before a pour or fire-stopping before ceilings close, are hold points that stop the work until an independent inspector releases them in writing. We engage the special inspectors ourselves, so they are independent of the contractor. We build mock-ups of the hardest details and test them first. Every failure is recorded on a nonconformance report and closed with evidence, and nothing is accepted as is without the designer's signature. Life-safety products are accepted only on tests of the exact assembly we are building, which is the lesson of Grenfell Tower. Prevention costs about one and a half percent of the budget, and our close-out review shows it repays itself many times over."

Score yourself: did you lead with evidence before covering, name hold points and independent inspection, and give the Grenfell lesson? If not, record it again tomorrow.

The corrected report, in outline

A report Cole would accept, still hypothetical, would show inspections by package with failures and re-inspections, NCRs by stage found and by age, each accept-as-is with the designer's signature attached, every hold point released with the inspector's name and time, special inspection engaged by the owner with the agency's own reports appended, every product substitution with its evidence and acceptance, and any missing test record with the investigation that replaced it. It would be prepared by the contractor and reviewed by the owner's representative, with both names on it. Every correction adds a name, a document or a date.

A practical exercise

Kema adds one exercise. Walk any building under construction, or study photographs of one, and point to three places where a defect would be buried by the next trade. For each, name the hold point that should sit there and the person who should release it. If you can do that quickly, you can read any inspection and test plan.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is a quality report that reads well and proves nothing. The control is owner-side review of the evidence behind it: the hold-point releases, the open NCR ages, the accept-as-is signatures and the special inspection reports.

The beginner's mistake

Treating a clean report with no failures as good news. Ask what was inspected, by whom, and why nothing was found.

Callback

In Week 83, Cole taught that independent reviews are worth only what their independence and scope allow. This week applied that to every layer of quality: the inspector, the certificate, the report. Independence is the first thing an auditor checks, and the first thing a budget cut removes.

Recap

Hold points stop the work. Mock-ups set the standard. NCRs record failure and must close with evidence. Special inspection is independent and owner-engaged. Products are accepted on tests of the exact assembly. Rule 116: a certificate is a claim, not evidence.

head: The six questions
speak: This week, quality. Quality is proved by evidence collected before work is covered. Each work package has an inspection and test plan, and the critical steps, like reinforcement before a pour or fire-stopping before ceilings close, are hold points: the work stops until an independent inspector releases it in writing. We engage the special inspectors ourselves, under the design professional's statement of special inspections, so they are independent of the contractor. Mock-ups test the hardest details first. Every failure goes on a nonconformance report and closes with evidence, and nothing is accepted as is without the designer's signature. Grenfell Tower taught that a certificate is a claim, so life-safety products are accepted only on tests of the exact assembly we are building. Prevention is the cheapest line in the cost of quality; defects found after handover are the most expensive. And a quality report with no failures makes me ask what was really inspected.
terms: Self-certification — a party inspecting and approving its own work without independent verification.
Closure discipline — the practice of closing nonconformances promptly with verified evidence and tracking their age.
Owner-side review — the owner's own check of the evidence behind a contractor's report.

hostile.q: Your contractor's quality report shows 140 inspections passed and no new defects. Why are you not satisfied?
hostile.a: Because a report with no failures usually means nothing is being found or nothing is being written down. I want the evidence behind it: who released each hold point, why a pour went ahead on the foreman's check, who signed off the waterproofing accepted as is, and why the contractor rather than the owner engaged the inspection agency. Until those are answered, the report is a claim, not evidence.
